About: Displacement Current — the Term That Rescued Ampère's Law

Source

Concept
Two surfaces bounded by the same Ampèrian loop give two different enclosed currents — the changing electric flux between the plates is exactly what reconciles them.
Simulation
Wire charging a parallel-plate capacitor; flat disc vs. bulging bag surface spanning one Ampèrian loop; toggle for Maxwell's displacement-current term.
Serves
Ampère–Maxwell law; motivation for displacement current; why EM waves need this term.
Misconception targeted
“Displacement current is a real current of something moving across the gap.” It is not — nothing crosses the gap; a changing electric flux produces the same magnetic field a current would.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The set-up

A wire carries a steady current I into a parallel-plate capacitor. Draw one Ampèrian loop round the wire. Ampère's law says the enclosed current is the same across any surface bounded by that loop.

Two such surfaces are drawn: a flat disc the wire pierces, and a bulging bag that slips past the wire and passes between the plates.

2 · Predict — can they ever agree?

With Ampère's original law only (conduction current, no Maxwell term), and any charging current you like: can the disc's tally and the bag's tally agree?

3 · Try it — Maxwell's term OFF

Drag the charging current slider. Watch the two tallies. The disc always reads exactly I; the bag always reads 0. Between the plates, the electric field grows as charge piles up — but with the Maxwell term off, that growth doesn't count as enclosed current.

Ampère's law contradicts itself: same loop, two answers.

4 · Switch Maxwell's term on

Toggle Maxwell's term ON. Now the bag's tally counts the changing electric flux between the plates as if it were a current: Id = ε₀ d ΦE/dt.

Sweep the current slider again. Read both tallies. They agree — not approximately, exactly — at every setting.

5 · What actually crosses the gap?

Nothing. No charge, no matter, no “displacement” of something across the gap. The name is Maxwell's, and it is misleading.

What's there is a changing electric flux. That change produces a magnetic field exactly as a current would — and, because of how a charging capacitor works, its magnitude equals the conduction current precisely. This is why the identity Id = I holds independently of the plate area or separation: it's built into charge conservation.

01

At a glance

A steady current charges a parallel-plate capacitor, and one loop is drawn round the wire. Two different surfaces are stretched over that loop, and the sim counts the current each one encloses, so you can test Ampère's law on a real case.

What you'll learn

  • How to count the current that passes through a surface bounded by a loop, and what Ampère's law says about that count.
  • What Maxwell's displacement-current term is, and how it is built from the electric flux between the plates.
  • How the displacement current depends on the charging current I and on the plate area and gap.
The wire pierces the disc. The bag bulges past the end of the wire and passes between the plates.

  • Flat disc (pink) and bulging bag (blue): the two surfaces bounded by that loop.
  • Electric field E (amber arrows) between the plates, with + and − charges on their inner faces.
  • Tallies: the current each surface encloses, in a banner on the canvas and in a sidebar panel.

03

With Ampère's original law the two surfaces disagree

Ampère's law ties the magnetic field B round a closed loop to the current the loop encloses:

∮ B · dℓ = μ₀ Ienc
B is the magnetic field and dℓ a small step along the loop.

The left side depends only on the loop, so every surface bounded by that loop should enclose the same current. In the original law only conduction current counts, which is what the sim shows with Maxwell's term OFF:

  • Flat disc: the wire pierces it, so it encloses the whole charging current I.
  • Bulging bag: it passes through the gap, where there is no wire and no charge flowing, so it encloses 0 A.

One loop gives two answers, and they differ by exactly I at every setting of the slider. Used this way, the original law contradicts itself.

See itSet I = 1.00 A with Maxwell's term OFF. Watch for: flat disc = 1.00 A, bulging bag = 0.00 A, and the tallies panel reading ✗ disagree by 1.00 A.
04

Maxwell's term lets the bag count the changing electric flux

Between the plates the electric field E grows as charge piles up. Maxwell added a term for that growth to Ampère's law:

∮ B · dℓ = μ₀ (Ienc + Id)
Id = ε₀ dΦE/dt
ΦE is the electric flux through the surface and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m.

Id is the displacement current. With the term ON it joins the bag's tally like a conduction current. The bag now counts the changing flux between the plates and reads the same as the disc, at every I.

The disc's tally does not change when the term is switched on. The wire still carries I through it.

See itSwitch Maxwell's term ON at I = 1.00 A. Watch for: the bag's tally matching the disc at 1.00 A, and the banner turning green: ✓ Ampère–Maxwell holds.
05

The displacement current equals I for any plates

For plates of area A holding charge Q, E = Q/(ε₀A), so the flux is ΦE = EA = Q/ε₀. The wire delivers charge at the rate dQ/dt = I. Therefore

Id = ε₀ dΦE/dt = dQ/dt = I
Charge conservation fixes the match.

Neither A nor the gap d appears, so this holds for any parallel-plate capacitor. Larger plates only make E change more slowly, since dE/dt = I/(ε₀A). In the sim, at I = 0.50 A:

QuantityValue
dΦE/dt = I/ε₀ (the canvas label)5.6 × 10¹⁰ V·m/s
dE/dt = I/(ε₀A), with A = 0.01 m²5.6 × 10¹² V/(m·s)
I

This slider moves the sim's I too.

See itSet I = 2.00 A with Maxwell's term ON. Watch for: both tallies at 2.00 A, and the flux-rate label reading 2.3 × 10¹¹ V·m/s, 4 times its value at 0.50 A.
06

Nothing crosses the gap

The name displacement current is misleading. It is not a flow of anything between the plates.

  • Charge arrives through the wire and collects on the inner faces of the plates. None crosses the vacuum gap.
  • What changes between the plates is the electric field E, so the electric flux through the bag changes.
  • A changing electric field produces a magnetic field in the same way a current does, and its size here equals I exactly.

So Id is a current only in the sense that matters to Ampère's law: it makes the same magnetic field. Together, the conduction current in the wire and Id in the gap form one unbroken current round the circuit.

See itStart charging at I = 0.50 A with Maxwell's term ON. Watch for: + and − signs building up on the plates and amber arrows lengthening between them, while the bag's tally stays at 0.50 A.
07

Where it matters

  • Electromagnetic waves. With Id, a changing E field makes a B field, and a changing B field makes an E field, so the two can sustain each other as a wave. Maxwell's equations give its speed as 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, the speed of light.
  • Capacitors in AC circuits. A capacitor passes an alternating current although no charge crosses its gap. In the gap, Id equals the current in the wires, so the current is continuous round the whole circuit.
  • Magnetic field inside a capacitor. There is a magnetic field between charging plates, as if the current I flowed through the gap.
08

Summary

In one line. Ampère's law counts the current through any surface bounded by a loop, and this sim tests it on one loop with two surfaces and a charging capacitor.

Key points

  • With conduction current only, the disc reads I and the bag reads 0 A, so Ampère's law contradicts itself.
  • Maxwell's term Id = ε₀ dΦE/dt fixes this: between the plates Id = I, whatever A and d are.
  • Nothing crosses the gap. A changing electric flux makes the magnetic field.

Common mix-ups

  • "Displacement current is charge crossing the gap." Nothing crosses. Only the electric field between the plates changes.
  • "Switching Maxwell's term on changes the disc's tally." The disc stays at I. Only the bag's tally changes, from 0 A to I.
  • "Bigger plates give a bigger displacement current." E changes more slowly, but Id = I stays the same.

Things to try on your own

  • With Maxwell's term OFF, set I to 0.05 A and then 2 A, and read the Agree? line each time.
  • With the term ON, move I to three values and check the two tallies match every time.
  • Read the flux-rate label at I = 0.50 A and 1.00 A, find the ratio, and predict the label at 2.00 A.
